sections.text: Shr blends three sounds smoothly into one: /s/ + /h/ + /r/. Say each word out loud and listen for that blended start.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The shrimp is on the bed.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Thr combines /th/ and /r/ right at the front of a word. Say each word out loud and listen for the blend.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: In sch words, the h is silent and the whole team of letters just makes the /sk/ sound. Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: When w comes before ar, it changes the vowel's sound completely — ar after w usually says /or/, as in "war" and "warm." Say each word out loud and listen closely.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: W also changes the sound of or — wor usually says /er/, as in "worm" and "world." Say each word out loud and listen for that twist.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: The ending -or often names a person who does something, like an actor or a visitor, and it says a quiet, unstressed /er/ sound. Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see a actor and a author.
A tailor is on the mat.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: -Er is the most common way to spell the /er/ sound at the end of a word, as in "camper" and "teacher." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: The suffix -ful means "full of" and is always spelled with just one l, even though it sounds like it could have two. Say each word out loud and listen for the ending.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The playful dog is hopeful for a treat.
This tool is useful and helpful.
I am thankful for my careful friend.
She is hopeful and thankful too.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: All keeps its own steady sound no matter which letter comes before it, as in "ball" and "small." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The tall wall is in the hall.
I can call Mom to walk.
Do not fall on the chalk.
I also almost lost the ball.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ull and ush both use the short /oo/-ish sound, as in "full" and "push." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The cup is full of water.
Pull the bull to the barn.
She sat on a soft cushion.
Don't be so pushy, just pull gently.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ai spells the long a sound in the middle of a word or syllable, as in "rain" and "train." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ay spells that same long a sound, but at the end of a word, as in "play" and "day." Ai and ay are a team — just used in different spots. Say each word out loud and listen.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ee is the most common way to spell the long e sound, as in "tree" and "sweet." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: At the end of a word, ey can also spell the long e sound, as in "key" and "money." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see a money on the table.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ea often spells the long e sound, as in "beach" and "read." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: A meat is on the mat.
A seat is on the mat.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ea usually spells long e, but watch for two tricky patterns: sometimes it spells short e, as in "bread," and sometimes long a, as in "great." Say each word out loud and listen closely.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The bread and the spread are here.
Get ready for a heavy day.
They got a steak for their break.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ie usually spells the long e sound, as in "field" and "chief" — think of the old rule "i before e." Say each word out loud and listen.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: At the end of a word, ie can also spell long i, as in "pie" and "tie." Say each word out loud and listen for the different sound.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Aw spells the /aw/ sound, usually at the end of a word or syllable, as in "saw" and "paw." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The saw is on the bed.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Au spells that same /aw/ sound, but in the middle of a word, as in "sauce" and "autumn." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: A cause is on the mat.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ow can spell the long o sound, as in "snow" and "grow." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ue spells the long u sound, as in "glue" and "blue." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see a true and a cue.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ew also spells the long u sound, as in "new" and "grew." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Oa spells the long o sound in the middle of a word, as in "boat," while oe spells it at the end, as in "toe." Say each word out loud and listen for the long o in both.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ow can also spell a completely different sound, the /ow/ diphthong, as in "cow" and "town." Same letters, new sound — say each word out loud and listen closely.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: A cow is on the mat.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Ou spells that same /ow/ diphthong, as in "cloud" and "sound." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Oo can spell a long, breathy /oo/ sound, as in "moon" and "food." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see a moon and a boot.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Oo can also spell a shorter sound, as in "book" and "look" — the very same two letters making a different sound. Say each word out loud and listen closely.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The hood and the book are here.
The hook and the foot are here.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Oi and oy spell the same /oy/ sound — oi in the middle of a word, as in "coin," and oy at the end, as in "boy." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: At the end of a longer word, y usually says long e instead, as in "happy" and "candy." Say each word out loud and listen for the difference.
At the end of most shorter words y usually makes the long i sound as in fly, try, dry. Say each word out loud and listen for the difference.
Y can make short i too when in the middle of words. Say each word out loud and listen for the difference.
The prefix a- at the start of a word is usually said quickly and softly, like /uh/, as in "awake" and "about." Say each word out loud and listen for that quiet beginning.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see a apart and a ahead.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: When c is followed by e, i, or y, it softens and says /s/ instead of its usual hard sound, as in "cent" and "city." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: When g is followed by e, i, or y, it can soften to say /j/, as in "page" and "giant." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The age is on the bed.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Dge also spells the /j/ sound, and it always follows a short vowel, as in "bridge" and "judge." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see a bridge on the table.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: In some words, t goes silent right after s, as in "listen" and "often." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing sound.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The fasten is on the bed.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: When b follows m at the end of a word, it stays silent, as in "comb" and "thumb." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing sound.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: L often goes silent before f, k, m, or v, as in "calf," "walk," and "calm." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing sound.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: At the end of a word, se can say /z/ instead of /s/, as in "cheese" and "choose." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: Do not pose and tease him.
She is as wise as he is.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: A final -le pairs a consonant with a quiet vowel sound to close out a word, as in "apple" and "table." Say each word out loud and listen for that last syllable.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: After a base word that ends in d or t, the ending -ed adds a whole new syllable, /ed/, as in "added" and "wanted." Say each word out loud and listen for the extra beat.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see a ended and a landed.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: After most other sounds, -ed is said simply as /d/, with no extra syllable, as in "played" and "called." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: When a syllable ends in a vowel with nothing after it, that vowel is "open" and usually says its own long name, as in "baker" and "paper." Say each word out loud and listen for it.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: A closed syllable ends with a consonant. Its vowel is short because it is trapped between consonants. To divide a word with two consonants between vowels, split between the consonants (VC/CV rule). This is the Rabbit Rule. Listen for the short vowel sounds and practice splitting.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The basket is on the table.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: An open syllable ends with a vowel. Its vowel is long because it is free at the end. To divide a word with one consonant between vowels, split before the consonant (V/CV rule). This is the Tiger Rule. Listen for the long vowel sounds and practice splitting.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The tiger is big and strong.
I have a piece of paper.
We will open the box now.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: The magic e (silent e) at the end of a syllable reaches back over one consonant to make the vowel say its long name. The e stays silent. In a VCe syllable, the vowel is long and the e is not heard. Notice how the vowel changes from short to long.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: We have hope for the future.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: A vowel team is two vowels working together to make one sound. They stay together in one syllable. Do not split them. The most common vowel teams are ai, ea, oa, ee, and ay. Listen for the long vowel sound the team makes.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The rain falls on the roof.
We row the boat on the lake.
I can see the sea from here.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: When a vowel is followed by r, the r controls the vowel and changes its sound. The vowel and r stick together in one syllable (Vr). Do not split them. Listen for the r-controlled sounds: ar, er, ir, or, and ur.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see a bird in the tree.
Use a fork to eat dinner.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: The consonant-le syllable is a final stable syllable at the end of a word. It sounds like /ul/. When dividing, split just before the consonant that comes before 'le'. This is the Turtle Rule. The vowel before 'le' is usually short.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: Put the book on the table.
I eat an apple every day.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Gh is tricky — in most words it's completely silent, as in "night," but in a smaller group it says /f/, as in "laugh." Say each word out loud and listen for which one it is.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The light is very bright at night.
I can fight for what is right.
He gave a sigh and said eight.
Do not laugh at the rough cough.
I have had enough of the tough fight.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Tion and sion both say /shun/ at the end of a word, as in "station" and "mission." Say each word out loud and listen for that same ending sound.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see a station and a action.
The mission is on the bed.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: -tion and -sion often sound like “shun” at the end of a word.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I put lotion on my hand.
The train is at the station.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Most words become plural by simply adding -s to the end, as in "cats" and "dogs." Say each word out loud and listen for the added /s/ or /z/ sound.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I see three birds in the trees.
Put the books on the shelf.
We need more cups and plates.
She has two hands full of lamps.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Words that end in a hissing sound like s, x, ch, or sh add -es to make them easy to say, as in "boxes." Words that end in a consonant plus y change the y to i and add -es, as in "baby" becoming "babies." Say each word out loud.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The foxes ran past the boxes.
She washed the dishes and cups.
Two buses stopped at the benches.
The babies played with the puppies.
Ladies bought candies at the shop.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Adding an apostrophe and s ('s) shows that something belongs to someone, as in "the dog's bone." If the word is already plural and ends in s, just add an apostrophe, as in "the dogs' toys." Say each phrase out loud.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The dog's bone is under the bed.
Mom's car is in the garage.
The boys' shoes are by the door.
My friends' house is down the street.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Add -er to compare two things, as in "faster," and -est to compare three or more, as in "fastest." Say each word out loud and listen for the ending.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: My dog runs faster than yours.
She is the tallest girl in class.
This box is smaller than that one.
He is the kindest boy I know.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: The prefix re- means "again," as in "redo," and the prefix un- means "not" or the opposite, as in "unhappy." Say each word out loud and listen for the beginning.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: She was unhappy about the unfair game.
Please unlock the door for me.
We need to unpack the boxes.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: The prefix dis- means "not" or "opposite of," as in "disagree," and the prefix pre- means "before," as in "preview." Say each word out loud and listen for the beginning.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: I disagree with my sister sometimes.
The magician made the rabbit disappear.
We need to prepare for the trip.
My little brother goes to preschool.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: The suffix -less means "without," as in "careless," and the suffix -ness turns a word into a feeling or state, as in "kindness." Say each word out loud and listen for the ending.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: Being careless can lead to accidents.
The room was full of darkness.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: The suffix -ment turns a verb into a noun, naming the result or action, as in "enjoyment" and "movement." Say each word out loud and listen for the ending.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: We felt great enjoyment at the park.
Please make your payment on time.
The excitement filled the whole room.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: A contraction joins two words together and uses an apostrophe to show missing letters. Not often shortens to n't, as in "isn't" and "don't." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing letters.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: We won't be late for school.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Contractions can also join a pronoun with will, have, or am, as in "I'll," "we've," and "I'm." Say each word out loud and listen for the missing letters.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Longer words often mix different syllable types together — closed, vowel team, and consonant-le. Break each word into syllables, say each part, then blend it into the whole word.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: The loud noise caused a disturbance.
Put the food in a plastic container.
The clowns will entertain the crowd.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word

sections.text: Some longer words combine r-controlled syllables with magic-e or open syllables, as in "afternoon" and "wonderful." Break each word into syllables, say each part, then blend it into the whole word.

sections.instruction: Read ALOUD and circle all words with the target sound
sentences: We will meet in the afternoon.
She had a wonderful time at the party.
This is a particular kind of flower.
He works in a different department.
It is important to be kind.

sections.title: A. Fill in the missing letters and say the word
